In summary, our research is concerned with
the modeling of charge carrier transport in III-nitrides.

the development of a self-consistent model of charge transport in polar and nonp polar multiple-quantum-well III-nitride light-emitting diodes which includes ballistic carrier transport and quantum-mechanical effects in the active region.
the development of a new generation of software tools for III-V optoelectronic device simulation which are based on the drift-diffusions and ballistic transport modeling.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ballistic transport model is an essential component of any drift-diffusion simulation tool for III-nitride light emitting devices and that it should be used for the purpose of design and optimization of these devices.
the drift diffusion model is sufficient for the modeling of polar III-nitride LEDs, but the model has to be extended to ballistic transport for the modeling of nonpolar III-Nitride LEDs.
the carrier transport in polar and nonpolarity III-nitrides is dominated by ballistic effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the drift-diffusions model is not suitable for modeling the carrier transport in the active region of the III-nitride LEDs.
ballistic transport effects should be included in the device modeling of III-nitride light emitting diodes.
ballistic carrier transport in polar and nonpolarity III-nitride devices can be neglected for the device performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in order to obtain a reliable description of the device operation one has to consider both drift-diffusion and ballistic carrier transport.
in order to correctly model carrier injection into opti- cally active QWs of III-nitride devices, the ballistic carrier transport must be taken into account.
the ballistic overshoot effect is essential for accurate modeling of III-nitride LEDs, particularly for the structures with high injection levels.
